p: Ana means to file in March, and the motion will land with Meredith Sloane, the chief deputy district attorney.
Ronnie Galvan, the bartender, still says her father swung first. He'd also swear her father walked out the back with nothing on his head, half an hour before the man in the cap.
At the bathroom sink Dani remembered something she'd never told anybody: the Sunday after, her father shaving at noon, with a scrap of tissue on his neck.
On the phone her father took her knight with his bishop, and told her again he drove straight home that night.
Teo pointed out that the man ran off on foot, and their father never walked anywhere he could drive.
Consuelo Baca. The neighbor across from the back lot, the State's eyewitness. She's eighty three now.
Alma Baca. Consuelo's granddaughter, a third grade teacher. She was eight that night, home sick with an earache.
Ana Brennan. Still working the case with Dani on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
Luis Ruiz. His bishop still sits on her knight's square, and neither of them brings it up.

Saturday, February 13. Consuelo Baca had called Ana's office three times on Tuesday and left three messages on the machine. Ana played them for Dani in order, standing by the desk with her arms folded, as if they were exhibits.

This is Consuelo Baca. I'll talk to the girl. Saturday, after the four o'clock Mass. A click. Then: Consuelo Baca again. Not after. Before. Two o'clock. My granddaughter says before. Then the third one, after a cough: Tell her come hungry.

I wrote her in January, Ana said. Letterhead. My name, my bar number, the works. She called back and asked for the girl. So you go alone, and you do the hardest thing there is to do with a witness. Which is? Nothing. Ask her what she saw. Then shut up. Write down her words, not yours.

Seventeen weeks to June. On Wednesday, February 3, Dani had made her move at last, and it wasn't the pawn. She'd brought a rook across instead, the long way, and on the other end of the line her father went so quiet she thought the call had dropped. Huh, he'd said. Last Wednesday he moved and she moved, and neither of them said a word about the bishop.

Thursday she'd told Teo on the phone where she'd be on Saturday. Across from the old lot. He'd said okay. Then he'd asked whether the floor down there was still wet, and she'd said it was fine, and he'd said it wasn't.
Dicta was asleep on the rug with her legs straight out, running somewhere. Ana stepped over her to get to the filing cabinet.

Ana came back from the cabinet with the dispatch log in its plastic sleeve and laid it on the desk next to Gene's notebook, still zipped in its freezer bag. She put one finger on the second line and kept it there.

Dispatch log, Saturday, October 27, 2007, page two. Eleven seventeen and thirty eight seconds: 911 call received. The caller, C. Baca, lives across from the rear lot of the Night Owl Tap, on Highway 2. Eleven seventeen and fifty two seconds: the caller says a male, red jacket, ball cap, struck the victim with an unknown object, and the subject fled on foot. Eleven eighteen and twenty seconds: the victim is down at the curb, not moving. Medical requested. Eleven eighteen and forty one seconds: unit two fourteen en route.

Before you sit in that woman's kitchen, you know to the word what she already said. Otherwise she'll tell you something old and you'll think it's new. Or she'll tell you something new and you'll miss it. What does this line state? Not what it means. What it says.

A man in a red jacket and a ball cap hit somebody and ran off on foot, Dani reads. That's it. That's the whole line. Ana lifts her finger. Red jacket. Ball cap. Struck. On foot. Four things, at eleven seventeen, from a woman with a sick kid and a phone in her hand. Anything she tells you today, check it against those four.

Specific detail. The line says the caller reported a male in a red jacket and ball cap who struck the victim with an unknown object and fled on foot. That's all four facts and nothing added. It records what she said, not that it happened.
Ana pulled Ronnie's statement from Phil's box and set it under the log, so the two times lined up. Eleven seventeen at the top. Eleven forty at the bottom.

Here's what I've got. Of every police paper we have, Ronnie's is the first one with your father's name on it. Twenty to twelve. The log is eleven seventeen. Take both times as right. She held up the pencil. Must be true. Not likely. Not probably. Must. What does that give you?
She said cap at 11:17, twenty three minutes before Pa's name is on any police paper we have.

So on paper, the cap comes first, Ana says. Before anybody wrote his name down, she'd already said cap. When she said cap there wasn't a name on any paper for it to help. That's not a probably. That's arithmetic. Why she said it is a different question. She writes 11:17 BEFORE 11:40 under CAP on the board, small.

Must be true. Join the two facts. The cap is in the log at eleven seventeen, and the name first appears at eleven forty. So on these papers the cap came first. Nothing is added and nothing is guessed.
Then Ana took a page out of Phil's trial binder and laid it beside the freezer bag. Gene's notebook on the left. The trial on the right.

Trial transcript, Monday, June 2, 2008, direct and cross examination of Consuelo Baca. Question: Mrs. Baca, where do you live? Answer: Across the street from the Night Owl. Behind it, across from the back lot. Question: Were you awake at about a quarter past eleven on the night of Saturday, October 27, 2007? Answer: Yes. My granddaughter had an earache. I was at the kitchen sink. Question: What did you see? Answer: A man hit another man by the curb, with something in his hand. The man fell down. The other one ran. Question: What was the man who ran wearing? Answer: A red jacket. Question: Did you see his face? Answer: No. I never saw his face. Question: What did you do? Answer: I called 911. Thank you, Mrs. Baca. Cross examination by Mr. Abrams. Question: Mrs. Baca, you can't tell this jury who that man was, can you? Answer: No, sir. Nothing further.
Seven questions, counting Phil's, Ana said. Read it against Gene's page. What did she tell somebody in 2007 that this page tells you nobody asked her in 2008?

What was the man who ran wearing? A red jacket. And the next question is about his face. Nobody asked, anything else? She'd said cap to dispatch, and cap to Gene, and the State had stopped one word short of it. So had Phil.

Inference. One open clothing question, one answer, and no follow up. Nobody asked "anything else?", so the cap she gave dispatch and Gene never came up. The transcript never says so. Read the questions and it's there.
Ana unzipped the freezer bag, the whole length of the seal, and turned the notebook to Consuelo's page, the one Gene started at five past nine. C. Baca, 64. And in the margin, in Gene's pencil, boy?

He wrote that on a Sunday morning, sitting with her, and in December he couldn't tell you why. She laid the pencil across the transcript at the second question, and Dani read it again under the lead. Were you awake at about a quarter past eleven on the night of Saturday, October 27, 2007? Now look where the questions start. Then tell me what that gives you.
Whatever she saw or heard before a quarter past eleven, nobody asked her about it.

A quarter past eleven, Ana says. First question after her address, and they put her at the sink at the moment they needed. Before that, the jury got nothing. If Gene's boy was anywhere, he was in the part nobody asked about.

Inference. The prosecutor's first question about the night begins at a quarter past eleven, and nothing goes earlier, on direct or cross. So the transcript implies she was never asked about anything before then.
She was early. She was always early. At 1:35 she parked on the far side of Highway 2, facing the vape shop that used to be the Night Owl, and turned off the engine and didn't get out.

The back lot was paved now, and striped. Six cars. A dumpster with a padlock. Across the street from it, small and yellow, with a chain link fence and a plaster Virgin by the steps, was the only house on the block.
Twenty five minutes. She opened the practice set on her phone, because that was what she did with twenty five minutes.

Practice set, question 9. Night nurse's log: The patient in Room 4 rang the call bell at 2:10, 2:40, and 3:15 A.M. Each time, the nurse found the window blind rattling in the draft from the heating vent and found nothing else wrong. Maintenance taped the blind down at 3:30. The patient did not ring again before the shift ended at 7:00 A.M. The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
Her mother had worked nights her whole life. Her mother would have taped the blind herself at 2:10 and not written it down.

Three rings, one rattle each time, nothing else wrong, and then the tape and no more rings. It doesn't prove the blind did it. It points there, and it points nowhere else. Most likely, at least part. The small words did the work.
Most strongly supported. The pattern backs a modest causal claim: the blind was likely involved. "Most likely" and "at least part" keep the claim inside what the log shows.

Alma Baca had the door open before Dani got to it. Twenty seven. Hair scraped back. Red pen behind one ear, uncapped. She looked at Dani the way she probably looked at a kid sent down to the office for somebody else's fight. She's eighty three. One hour. If she gets tired, you go. Okay. I mean it. I know you do.

The kitchen smelled like cumin and the comal. Consuelo Baca was small and straight in a cardigan buttoned to the neck, and she didn't let Dani say one word until there was a bowl of albóndigas in front of her and a tortilla on top of the bowl to keep it warm. Eat. Then. Alma sat at the end of the table with a stack of spelling tests and didn't grade one of them.
Dani ate. Then she asked what she'd come to ask, and only that. What did you see.

Consuelo told it looking at the window over the sink, not at Dani. The sink, the earache, the man by the curb, the thing in his hand. The detective asked me how tall. I told him I couldn't say. I couldn't. There was nothing out there to measure him by. She turned her hands over on the table. Only the other one. The other one was a big man. Big in the shoulders. And this one was smaller than him. That I saw. Smaller.
So he was smaller than the man he hit. That's what you could see.

Yes. Consuelo nods once, hard, like a drawer shutting. Smaller than the big one. That's all. Write that. Dani writes SMALLER THAN THE BIG ONE. It fits her father. It fits half the men in Adams County. That's what it's worth, and she writes it at that size.
Most strongly supported. Her account backs one comparison, the attacker against the victim. It doesn't give a height and it doesn't rule anyone in or out. Dani keeps it exactly that size.
And before. Before the one in the jacket. Consuelo said it almost in passing. The little boy.

Ten minutes to eleven, by the stove. Alma's drops were at eleven, every four hours, and I was watching the clock for them. Out there in the lot. Papi. Papi. Like that. She said it softly, in a small voice, and it was worse than if she'd said it loud. Not screaming. Past screaming. You know how they get. I went to the glass. At night, with the light on in here, all you see is yourself and the stove. Out there, the trucks, dark. Then she was crying for me too, so I went to her.

I told the young policeman at the door. He wrote in his little book and he said, that's some kid from the apartments, ma'am. Some neighbor's kid. I said, what neighbor's kid is out at eleven o'clock in the back of a bar on a Saturday, crying for his papi? He said, yes ma'am. She shrugged. The detective wrote it too, the next day. Then nobody asked me again. Not ever.
Boy? In the margin. Nineteen years in a gun safe.
So a little boy was out there in the lot that night, crying for his papi.
Yes. That. Dani writes it down. BOY. PAPI. 10:50. She underlines 10:50 twice, and she doesn't write anything else.
Most strongly supported. What she heard backs a child in the lot, in distress, calling "Papi." That's the claim at the size of the evidence. It names no one, and it doesn't say why he was crying.
Ten to eleven. Teo was at Abuela's. Everybody knew where Teo was.
Consuelo got up and took Dani's bowl to the sink, and stood there with it, looking out. Come see.

It was a small window. A geranium in a coffee can, a dish rack, the plaster Virgin's twin on the sill, faded to the color of milk. Through the glass, the paved lot. The new curb. A row of parking stripes. At the curb stood a light pole, and on the pole, zip tied at about shoulder height, were two purple Rockies pennants, one faded nearly pink and one under it still dark.

His sister, Consuelo said, before Dani could ask. Every October. She never knocks. I leave the porch light on so she can see to do the ties. Dani had never thought of anybody standing at that curb on purpose. She'd seen his sister once, across a courthouse hall in 2008, with her purse in both hands. Dani had been the one who looked away.

The refinery men parked there in a row. Every Saturday. Trucks, trucks, trucks. And he ran that way. She pointed with the bowl. North. Past the end of the stripes there was a chain link fence with a gap in it, and past the fence a ditch, a long gray trough of ice and dead cattails, and past the ditch the rail bed, raised up on its gravel, and the tracks. Past the tracks, a long way off, the refinery. Its lights never go off. In the daytime you can hardly see them. Nothing in between. No street. No driveway. Nowhere a truck could go.

There's nothing back there. The ditch. The tracks. The kids go back there to drink. The young policeman and the other one walked it that night with their flashlights, all the way to the tracks. They didn't find anybody. Not a thing in his hand, not a thing on the ground.

In January, on the basement floor, Teo had said on foot, and men with trucks drive, and she'd wondered what was north of that lot. She didn't need a map now. She put it the way Ana would, only what had to be true: the man ran north on foot, and north there's nowhere to drive.

If. That's all she gets to keep, and it's enough. The State's man ran away from a row of trucks into a ditch, and the State's man drove a truck. Nobody in 2008 had to explain that. North was a word in a report. Nobody stood at this sink and looked. She writes NORTH, NO ROAD and dates it.

Must be true. Whoever ran north went where no truck could go. So if the man was Luis, he went where his truck couldn't follow. That's guaranteed by the facts, and it's conditional. It doesn't claim the man wasn't Luis.
Back at the table. The clock, Dani said. Just that. What time, and how she knew it.

That one. The stove: white enamel gone yellow at the knobs, a clock set in the back panel, its second hand still going round. Ten to eleven, the boy. I was watching it for the drops. Eleven, drops. Then I sat on her bed and sang her the whole song. Twice. Three times. Till she quit. She smiled down the table at Alma, who was reading one spelling test very hard. Then up to rinse the dropper. That's when. At the sink.
Did you hear the boy again? No. Not after. I listened. I sang and I listened.
So whatever made him cry happened before eleven, before the man in red.

Yes, Consuelo says. Before. A long time before. Three songs' worth. Dani draws it like Ana would, a line and two ticks. 10:50, boy. 11:15, jacket. Two things on one night, and half an hour between them that nobody ever wrote down.
Most strongly supported. Boy at about 10:50. Attack after the eleven o'clock drops. So whatever set him off came first. That much the clock gives you. Not why.

Ten to three. Alma had looked at the stove clock twice, and the third time she said Abuela in the voice you'd use on a third grader stalling at the pencil sharpener. Consuelo waved her off. Dani was putting the cap back on her pen, and before she could close the notebook Consuelo leaned over and set a hand on it.

You were the girl, she said. At the courthouse. In the hall, in that blue dress. Somebody should have hemmed those sleeves. Dani said she remembered the dress. Her mother had bought it the night before, on sale, a size up so it would last. I read what you said in the paper, Consuelo said. The jacket and the washer.

All I said was red. I said it to the police and I said it to the jury, and then the man in the tie got up and said it ten more times, and every time he said it he got closer to your father's name. She looked straight at Dani for the first time since the door. They used my words too, mija.
You told them what you saw. They're the ones who said whose jacket it was.

Yes, Consuelo says, and holds on to Dani's wrist for a second. That's right. I said red. I never said a name, not one time, and I'd swear to that in front of anybody. At the far end of the table Alma pushes her chair back, goes to the sink, and stands there running the tap with her back to them.
Would agree with. She says it: "I said red," and the name came from someone else. Dani's reply puts the line where Consuelo puts it. What she saw, her side. Who it was, theirs.

At the door Consuelo put a hand on each side of Dani's face, the way you'd check a child for fever. Yours too, mija. They used yours too. Dani thanked her. She'd meant it when she said it to Consuelo. Coming back the other way, she couldn't take it.
Alma walked her out. On the porch she pulled the door shut behind them, almost all the way, and spoke low.

She went to confession every Saturday for a year after that trial. Every Saturday. She hadn't done anything. She looked across the street at the lot. Don't bring her into this for nothing. It isn't for nothing. Alma held her eyes a second longer than was comfortable. I remember the song, she said. Nothing else. I've tried. For her, I've tried. She went back in.

In the car Dani left the engine running for the heat and called Ana. She read her the notebook page, her own, word for word. Smaller. Papi. Ten to eleven. North, and nothing back there. When she got to Papi, Ana didn't say anything for long enough that Dani heard Dicta's tags rattle somewhere behind her.

Her words, Ana said finally. Write all of it out tonight. Hers. Not yours. Then, briskly: Now the record. What the jury had. Ronnie, out the back at a quarter to eleven. Consuelo, a man in red at the curb at a quarter past. The State, that man was your father. Take all three as true. What has to be?
That Pa was near the lot, or back at it, half an hour after he left the bar.
Line four, Ana says. Near the lot at 11:15. Nobody ever proved it. They didn't have to. If all three are true it just is, and the jury filled in the half hour by itself.
Must be true. If he went out the back at 10:45 and he was the man at the curb at 11:15, then at 11:15 he was there, whether he stayed or returned. Nothing more is needed, and nothing more follows.

Now his, Ana said. Say your father's right. He was in the truck and gone before eleven, and he didn't come back that night. And say Consuelo's right about a quarter past. Put them side by side. Which of these can't be true?
Over at the house the front curtain moved. Alma, checking. It didn't close all the way.
That Pa was the man who hit Travis at the curb and ran north on foot.

That's the one, Ana says. And it's why nobody in 2008 ever put a minute on when he drove away. Pick any minute before 11:15 and they'd need him coming back. They never had to say it, so they never did.

Must be false. If he was gone before eleven and never came back, he wasn't at the curb at a quarter past. So he can't be the man Consuelo saw. Take both accounts as true, and it's the one claim that can't be.

Quarter to four, the door. Alma, and her grandmother in the good coat, for the four o'clock. Alma reached back in and hit the porch light, for later. Consuelo saw the car. One hand up, small, like at a bus stop. Dani put hers up too.
She didn't go home. Two miles, and she couldn't. Up Highway 2 to the refinery gate, turn around in the gravel, back down past the lot, up again. Radio off. Till the light went.

It was dark by the time she turned onto her own street, a little before six. The streetlight in front of the house had been flickering since Christmas, and in one of the flickers she saw it, and drove past her own driveway, and had to back up.

The washer was on the curb. The old one. Avocado green, the color of the whole house in 1990, sitting on a flattened box by the mailbox with its lid shut and its hoses coiled on top. A strip of duct tape across the front, in black marker, in capitals she'd know anywhere. LEAKS.

She went in through the side door and down the stairs without taking her coat off. The floor at the bottom was dry. It had been wet for a month and now it was dry, mopped, and there was a white washer where the green one had been, not new, a few years old, with a scuff on one corner and the hoses tightened down and the whole thing level. The shop vac was gone. On the lid, folded in a square, was one of his shop rags.
A text from Teo. that thing was leaking. dont make it a thing
She read it standing in the basement. In her head Consuelo was still saying smaller, smaller than the big one, the only measurement she'd ever been willing to give. She read Teo's text again.

She went back out to the curb. Cold enough now that the box under it had frozen to the grass. Her hand on the lid. Fifteen, a Sunday, eight in the morning: this lid, this drum, a red sleeve stuck to the side of it. And later, in a room full of strangers, because it was true. In the washer, downstairs. It was wet. The cycle was done.
She lifted it. Empty. No, one sock. Hers, gray, plastered to the drum since January probably. Into the coat pocket.
Inside: the bathroom towels, the dish towels off the oven door, his rag. All of it in together. The dial turned the wrong way, the opposite of the old one, which cost her a minute and one bad word.
It filled quiet. The old one used to bang like somebody was locked in it. Two steps up from the bottom, her Wednesday step. She watched the concrete.

Phone out, after a while. Thank you, she typed, and looked at it, and killed it. Ok. Sent. Then the notebook on her knee and Consuelo's words, all of them, Consuelo's and not hers, the way Ana wanted, while the water ran.
She stayed till the spin cycle. To be sure. Nothing came out from under it.
